summary: Zeghidour frames the talk around the 'Her' movie analogy, acknowledging it's overused yet relevant because the film anticipated natural voice interaction 13 years ago. He introduces Gradium AI as a foundational voice model provider building speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and speech-to-speech building blocks — not orchestration or vertical solutions. Gradium spun off from a non-profit lab funded by Eric Schmidt, Xavier Niel, and others, which produced Moshi, speech-to-speech translation, and Pocket TTS. He demonstrates voice cloning requiring only 10 seconds of audio, then contrasts current demos (11 Labs, Richmini) with the 'Her' ideal, noting latency remains high, simultaneous speech isn't handled, and systems are essentially text models with a voice wrapper — losing paralinguistic information. On cascaded architectures, even fast TTS alone exceeds 200ms, while human conversation requires the entire stack within ~200ms. Tool calls add 500ms–4s of unpredictable latency, becoming the dominant bottleneck. He shows a 'filler' approach where the LLM sends a tool call and keeps conversation flowing naturally while waiting for results. He distinguishes speech-to-speech from cascaded systems, noting it reduces latency but remains half-duplex in all cases except Moshi. Half-duplex models can't handle overlap or backchanneling — essential to human conversation (up to 20% overlap in Japanese). The Moshi full-duplex demo shows natural overlapping speech, and Zeghidour confirms it remains the most robust conversational experience to date. However, he is candid about Moshi's limitations: it was 'very stupid,' had no tool calls, no agent capability, no observability, and no real paralinguistic understanding despite technically preserving audio information. He argues full-duplex models need the same reliability, intelligence, and personalization as cascaded systems before they can replace them. On scalability, he notes voice is expensive — hyperscalers run voice mode at a loss, TTS is the dominant cost, and teams have burned through fundraising on TTS bills before growing a user base. Privacy is another driver toward local processing. Gradium's response is Phonon, an on-device TTS model under 100M parameters running on smartphone CPU, better than existing on-device alternatives like Kokoro (which lacks voice cloning). He concludes that voice is not a commodity — the last mile requires science and engineering, not prompt engineering.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Cascaded voice AI systems (STT→LLM→TTS) are architecturally incapable of human-like latency: even fast TTS alone exceeds the ~200ms total human response budget.
Tool calls have become the dominant latency bottleneck at 500ms–4s, making TTS latency optimization comparatively irrelevant for real tasks.

Full-duplex conversation (simultaneous listening and speaking) is essential to natural interaction; Moshi demonstrated this is solvable but the model was not useful — no tools, no observability, no agent capability.
Full-duplex models won't replace cascaded systems until they match them in reliability, intelligence, and personalization — Zeghidour concedes cascaded systems are 'so practical and so convenient.'
TTS is the dominant cost in voice AI; teams have burned through fundraising on TTS bills before achieving user growth, and hyperscalers run voice mode at a loss.

Paralinguistic understanding — tone, hesitation, discomfort — is preserved in speech-to-speech models but not exploited unless training data and objectives specifically target it; cascaded systems lose this information entirely at transcription.
Gradion Phonon is an on-device TTS model under 100M parameters running on smartphone CPU, addressing cost and privacy barriers for consumer voice apps.
Voice is not a commodity — the last mile to 'Her' requires science and engineering, not prompt engineering.
Gradium AI positions itself as a foundational voice model provider, not an orchestration or vertical-specific company.
Understand the architectural limitations of cascaded voice AI systems versus speech-to-speech models

sections.title: Introduction and Gradium AI mission
sections.summary: Zeghidour introduces Gradium AI as a foundational voice model provider (STT, TTS, speech-to-speech) for builders of voice agents, explicitly not doing orchestration or vertical solutions.

sections.title: Voice cloning demonstration
sections.summary: Demonstrates voice cloning of podcaster Joel from ~10 seconds of audio. Notes Gradium spun off from a non-profit lab funded by Eric Schmidt, Xavier Niel, and others, which developed Moshi, speech-to-speech translation, and Pocket TTS.

sections.title: The 'Her' analogy and current Voice AI limitations
sections.summary: Uses the 'Her' movie (13 years old) as a reference for natural voice interaction. Shows 11 Labs and Richmini demos, noting latency remains high, simultaneous speech isn't handled, and systems are essentially text models with voice — paralinguistic information is lost.

sections.title: Cascaded systems and latency challenges
sections.summary: Explains cascaded architecture (STT→LLM→TTS). Even fast TTS exceeds 200ms alone, while human conversation requires the entire stack within ~200ms. Tool calls add 500ms–4s, becoming the dominant bottleneck, making TTS optimization (10–20ms) comparatively irrelevant.

sections.title: Filler approach and live travel agent demo
sections.summary: Introduces fillers: LLM sends tool call and keeps conversation flowing naturally while waiting, then reinserts results. Live demo of a travel agent (Wanderlust Travel) that says nice things about Tokyo while retrieving booking options.

sections.title: Speech-to-speech vs cascaded and half-duplex limitations
sections.summary: Clarifies speech-to-speech as a single model (audio in, audio out) reducing latency but remaining half-duplex in all cases except Moshi. Half-duplex can't handle overlap or backchanneling (up to 20% in Japanese). Demonstrates a half-duplex model failing annoyingly when backchanneling occurs.

sections.title: Moshi full-duplex demonstration
sections.summary: Shows Moshi full-duplex demo with co-founder Alex, where overlapping speech about plotting a trajectory to planet Sirius 22 is handled naturally — demonstrating that full-duplex conversation is solvable.

sections.title: Paralinguistic understanding and Moshi's limitations
sections.summary: Continues Moshi demo showing robustness to noise and multiple speakers. Shows a Her movie clip illustrating paralinguistic understanding — AI detects character discomfort from tone. Explains that speech-to-speech models technically preserve this information but don't exploit it unless trained for it. Candidly admits Moshi was 'very stupid' — no tool calls, no agent capability, no observability, not production-ready. Concludes full-duplex models need reliability, intelligence, and personalization matching cascaded systems before they can replace them.

sections.title: Scalability, cost, and privacy challenges
sections.summary: Discusses scalability: voice is expensive, hyperscalers run voice mode at a loss. TTS is the dominant cost — teams have burned fundraising on TTS bills before growing user base. LLM and STT are cheap; TTS consumes most cost. Privacy concerns drive demand for local processing, with users increasingly wanting private data kept on-device.

sections.title: Gradion Phonon: on-device TTS and conclusion
sections.summary: Introduces Gradion Phonon: on-device TTS running on smartphone CPU, under 100M parameters, better than existing on-device models like Kokoro (which lacks voice cloning). Demos with Rick and Morty voices. Goal is enabling consumer voice apps that scale without API costs. Concludes voice is not a commodity — the last mile to 'Her' requires science and engineering. Invites people to join Gradium.
